speaker: Bryan Cantrill
title: The history of servers, the cloud, and what’s next – with Oxide
question: In large-scale distributed systems, why can't fault-tolerant software fully compensate for cheap, unreliable server hardware?
guest: Early on, they had this idea that it doesn't matter what junk hardware we run on because our software is going to run as a distributed system—we don't need protected memory because it doesn't matter if your DIMMs fail. What they learned is that it does matter. If your DIMMs fail outright, that's actually not a problem. If your memory silently returns the wrong thing—rampant data corruption—that is a problem. Next thing you know, your software inserts that corrupted value into a row in a database, and now you've got a correctness problem. They overshot the mark. Once the business was established enough, they stopped Velcroing cheap machines together and engineered custom warehouse-scale machines—with DC busbars and proper power architecture—going from being too cheap for Dell or Supermicro to being much better engineered than those systems ever were.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Fault-tolerant software can only handle failures it can detect, and it relies on some minimum level of correct behavior from the hardware underneath it. That creates several limits.

First, software tolerates fail-stop faults well (a machine dies, a replica takes over), but cheap hardware also produces silent faults: memory bit flips without ECC, disks or CPUs that return wrong results without reporting errors. Corrupted data can be replicated, checkpointed and propagated before anything notices, so redundancy spreads the damage rather than masking it. This is why Google's Barroso and Hölzle argue that hardware must at least detect and report its faults, even if software handles recovery.

Second, tolerance mechanisms assume failures are rare and independent. Unreliable hardware raises the odds of overlapping or correlated failures (bad batches, shared power or firmware) that exceed the replication level.

Third, recovery is not free. Re-replication, rebuilds and retries consume bandwidth, compute and operator time, and constant repair degrades performance and tail latency.

Finally, the fault-tolerance software is itself complex, and frequent failures exercise rare, buggy recovery paths. Beyond some failure rate, the cost of redundancy, repair and complexity exceeds what was saved on hardware.

models.answer:
Fault-tolerant software primarily assumes clean, independent crashes, whereas cheap, unreliable hardware frequently fails in subtler ways. Without safeguards like ECC memory or enterprise storage controllers, low-grade components suffer silent data corruption: bit flips and CPU miscalculations alter data before software checksums are computed, allowing bad state to replicate across healthy nodes as valid writes. Cheap hardware also exhibits "gray" or slow failures, where degrading drives, throttling processors, or flaky network cards pass heartbeat checks while severely inflating tail latency across dependent services.

Even when nodes crash cleanly, high failure rates trap clusters in perpetual recovery. Constant leader elections and data rebuilding consume network and I/O bandwidth, hurting normal performance and shrinking the safety window before concurrent or batch-correlated failures exhaust redundancy quorums. Moreover, recovery code paths are complex and disproportionately harbor latent software bugs that turn routine hardware faults into cascading outages. Finally, total cost of ownership favors baseline hardware quality: overprovisioning spare capacity and paying technicians to continually diagnose and replace broken servers quickly erases upfront hardware savings.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Fault-tolerant software works by detecting failures and then retrying, replicating, or rerouting around them. It can't fully make up for cheap hardware for a few reasons, a point made in Barroso and Hölzle's *The Datacenter as a Computer*.

First, software can only handle faults it can see. If hardware fails silently, for example with memory bit-flips, CPU miscalculations, or disk corruption that no ECC or checksum catches, the result can be bad data that spreads through replicas and gets returned to users. Hardware has to make errors detectable before software can recover from them.

Second, failures cost money even when they're handled well. Every failed component needs a technician, a replacement part, and time out of service. Recovery also uses extra capacity for redundancy, re-replication traffic, and repeated computation. Past a certain failure rate, these costs cancel out the savings from cheaper parts.

Third, high failure rates make the software harder to build. Recovery code gets more complex and harder to test, and it slows down developers. Frequent or correlated failures, such as a whole rack or power domain going down at once, can overwhelm replication and cause tail latency.

So the goal is hardware that is good enough: errors that are detectable and failure rates low enough that software can handle them cheaply.

Rather than failing cleanly, low-grade components often exhibit silent data corruption—such as memory bit flips, defective CPUs, or misdirected disk writes—and "gray" or fail-slow behaviors like intermittent packet drops or sluggish drives. If failures occur faster than the system can recover, or several replicas fail together because they share a power supply, rack, or hardware defect, the system can lose availability or data.

Even when recovery succeeds, it consumes resources. Retries add load, rebuilding replicas uses network and disk bandwidth, and spare capacity costs money. Hardware that silently corrupts data also poses a harder problem than hardware that simply stops responding, because the software must detect the corruption before it can recover. Cheap servers can make economic sense, but only if the system can absorb their failure rate and recovery costs while meeting its reliability targets.

Failover shifts work to surviving servers, and rebuilding lost replicas consumes network bandwidth and disk I/O. If failures happen faster than the system can recover, it can run short of capacity or lose enough replicas to make data unavailable or permanently lost.

Hardware failures can also be correlated. A shared power supply or a defective batch of drives can take out several replicas at once. Some faults are harder to detect than a crash, such as a drive silently returning corrupted data. Software can mitigate these risks with checksums and replicas spread across independent failure domains, but those safeguards cost money and still depend on enough healthy hardware. Cheap servers can make economic sense, provided their failure rates and recovery costs fit the service’s reliability goals.
